query: Which material can be used for to improve the ductility and toughness of the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy (HEAs), and why?

generation.hypothesis: Adding Nb to the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy will improve its ductility and toughness compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A HfZrTi high-entropy alloy produced by arc melting that exhibits a predominantly brittle BCC or mixed phase microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce Nb as an additional alloying element into the HfZrTi composition during arc melting synthesis.
generation.conditions: Systematic variation of Nb content under controlled processing conditions to ensure homogeneous phase distribution; testing conducted at room temperature (with potential extension to cryogenic temperatures) using standard tensile and fracture toughness evaluations along with SEM/TEM microstructural analysis.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a more ductile phase or modification of the phase distribution (e.g., stabilization of a ductilizing solid solution) that reduces stress concentrations.
generation.mechanism: Nb addition is expected to alter the phase stability and/or promote a more homogeneous, potentially single-phase structure, reducing the formation of brittle intermetallic phases. This modification in the microstructure facilitates dislocation motion and absorbs deformation energy, thereby enhancing ductility and toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved tensile ductility and fracture toughness, with a measurable increase in strain-to-failure and energy absorption before fracture when compared to the baseline HfZrTi alloy.
generation.baseline: HfZrTi HEA without Nb addition, which is assumed to have lower ductility and toughness due to its inherent brittle microstructural features.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected within a specific range of Nb addition; excessive Nb may lead to phase separation or other detrimental effects. Additionally, the magnitude of improvement may depend on the precise processing parameters and testing temperature.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Nb content for maximum improvement is not precisely known and may vary with processing conditions. The exact size of the ductility and toughness improvements is also uncertain and requires experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HfZrTi-based alloys with incremental additions of Nb (e.g., 0, 2, 5, and 10 at.% Nb) using arc melting to ensure homogeneous compositions. Perform microstructural analysis using SEM and TEM to verify phase stability and distribution. Conduct tensile tests and fracture toughness measurements at room temperature (and optionally at cryogenic temperatures) to quantify improvements in ductility and toughness. Compare the mechanical properties of Nb-modified alloys with the baseline HfZrTi alloy.
measurements: Tensile stress-strain curves (to determine strain-to-failure, yield strength, and ultimate tensile strength)
Microstructural characterization (phase identity and distribution via SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Nb does not lead to a statistically significant improvement in tensile ductility and fracture toughness, or if it produces deleterious phase formation that compromises mechanical integrity relative to the baseline HfZrTi alloy, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted a lot of attention in recent years, due to the unique combinations of structural, physical and chemical properties of these alloys [1] – [3] . HEAs usually form simple structures such as body-centered cubic (BCC) (e.g. TaNbHfZrTi [4] , NbTaVWZr [5] etc.) or face-centered cubic (FCC) (e.g., CoCrCuFeNi [6] , CoCrFeMnNi [7] etc.) solid solutions. The large number of the alloying elements in near-equiatomic proportions result in high configurational entropy in these solid solutions. However, these alloys can decompose to multiple phases upon changing the composition or annealing at different temperatures or a combination of both [8] – [10] . Such a phase decomposition is often the result of the complex interplay of configurational entropy of mixing with the enthalpies of mixing of the constituent elements. Additionally, such multiphase microstructures are more likely to exhibit the desired properties for real engineering applications. Hence, tuning the composition and fractions of phases is critical for achieving the desired properties [10] , [11] .
